docs.title: Privacy Skill Vault
docs.text:
A personal cybersecurity portfolio, lab notebook, and practical knowledge base.

I work across cyber-fraud monitoring, security operations, and technical investigation. Privacy Skill Vault is where I document the concepts I study, the environments I build, the tools I test, and the investigation methods I refine.

The goal is straightforward: make technical work understandable, reproducible, and honest about what has actually been tested.

About me Explore the learning paths

01 / LEARN

Structured notes across infrastructure, monitoring, offensive security, investigations, and operations.

02 / BUILD

Lab environments, experiments, configurations, troubleshooting, and validation notes.

03 / ANALYSE

Defensive investigation walkthroughs, evidence handling, detection logic, and clearly labelled scenarios.

04 / USE

Browser-based utilities and operational references for SOC and security analysis.

docs.title: How information is labelled
docs.text:
Accuracy matters more than presentation. Content is identified by its evidence level:

  • Professional experience — generalised and sanitised descriptions; no employer, customer, or internal system details.
  • Lab-tested — performed in a controlled environment, with relevant setup and limitations recorded.
  • Simulated scenario — constructed for learning; not represented as a real incident.
  • Research note — based on documentation or external references and not yet independently validated.

docs.title: Current areas of focus
docs.text:
Cyber-fraud detection and investigation, SIEM monitoring, endpoint and network telemetry, detection engineering, Linux and Windows operations, and controlled security testing.

This is a personal learning and portfolio site. It does not represent an employer, disclose confidential operational information, or provide evidence of a real incident unless a page explicitly says so.

docs.title: About
docs.text:
I'm a cybersecurity professional working across cyber-fraud monitoring, fraud analysis, security operations, and technical investigation.

My current work focuses on monitoring fraud-protection systems, analysing suspicious activity, investigating alerts, tuning prevention controls, and supporting the reliability of security platforms. I also bring SOC analyst experience and continue to develop practical skills through structured study and controlled labs.

docs.text:
• Cyber-fraud detection, prevention, and investigation
  • Account and transaction activity analysis
  • Security monitoring, alert triage, and escalation
  • SIEM workflows and detection tuning

  • Security platform operations and troubleshooting

docs.title: Technologies and tools
docs.text:
Tools I have worked with or studied include Group-IB Fraud Protection, Elastic Stack, Splunk, Linux, Windows, PowerShell, Wazuh, Suricata, Zeek, Sysmon, Wireshark, Nmap, Burp Suite, and related security tooling.

This list is not a claim that every tool is used in production. Individual write-ups identify the environment and whether a technique was professionally used, lab-tested, or researched.

docs.title: Why this site exists
docs.text: I use this space to keep technical notes organised, record what worked and what did not, and turn isolated troubleshooting or investigation lessons into reusable references. The emphasis is on practical understanding rather than presenting a long list of tools or inflated claims.

docs.title: Responsible disclosure and privacy
docs.text:
Examples are sanitised or simulated. I do not publish customer data, account identifiers, internal IP addresses, employer-confidential information, or operational screenshots that could expose systems. Security testing content is intended only for systems you own or are explicitly authorised to assess.

For feedback or professional contact, use the public contact details linked from my professional profile.

docs.title: Blog
docs.text:
Technical articles and longer write-ups will be listed here when they are complete and reviewed.

The blog is separate from structured learning paths:

New articles will be published on this domain so readers have one consistent destination. An empty publication list is better than linking to placeholder articles.

docs.title: Investigations
docs.text: Defensive investigation methods and worked examples covering security alerts, endpoint activity, network evidence, and cyber-fraud signals.

docs.title: Evidence standard
docs.text: Every report must distinguish observed evidence from interpretation. Published material is classified as sanitised professional experience, lab investigation, simulated scenario, or research note. No customer records, internal banking details, production IP addresses, or employer-confidential information belong here.

docs.title: Detailed walkthrough
docs.text: • Suspicious PowerShell from a Scheduled Task — a synthetic evidence-led investigation with competing hypotheses, correlation steps, and an analyst checklist.

docs.title: Worked example: suspicious PowerShell launched by a scheduled task
docs.text:
SIMULATED TRAINING SCENARIO

Hostnames, timestamps, commands, and indicators in this example are synthetic. It does not describe a real customer, employer, or production incident.

docs.title: Initial alert
docs.text: A monitoring rule flags encoded PowerShell launched by a scheduled-task process outside an expected maintenance window.

docs.title: Investigation questions
docs.text:
1. What process created PowerShell, and what was its full command line?
  2. Which account and integrity level were involved?
  3. Is the scheduled task known, approved, and correctly owned?
  4. Do script-block, process, DNS, proxy, and firewall records corroborate the activity?
  5. Is there evidence of payload retrieval, persistence, lateral movement, or impact?

docs.title: Evidence to correlate
docs.text:
• Process creation telemetry, including parent process and command line
  • PowerShell operational events where logging is enabled
  • Scheduled-task registration and execution history
  • DNS and network connection records
  • File creation, hash, signature, and reputation context
  • Change records and owner confirmation

docs.title: Example reasoning
docs.text: An encoded command is a triage signal, not proof of malware. A scheduled task can be legitimate administration or unauthorised persistence. Validate the task definition, executable path, script contents, account, creation time, change history, and network destinations before assigning a verdict.

docs.title: Possible outcomes
docs.text:
• Expected administration: document the owner and maintenance purpose; tune narrowly with evidence.
  • Policy violation: remediate the configuration even if malicious intent is not established.
  • Likely compromise: follow incident-response procedures, preserve evidence, and consider containment under organisational policy.
  • Insufficient evidence: state what telemetry is missing and what additional collection is required.

Avoid treating one event or one indicator as a complete story. Record confidence, alternative explanations, data gaps, and the basis for every conclusion.

docs.title: Investigation Walkthrough: Suspicious PowerShell from a Scheduled Task
docs.text:
Simulated training scenario

This case is synthetic. Host names, timestamps, users, event records, and command lines are invented for training. It is not a description of a real customer, employer, bank, or production incident.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
An endpoint alert reports PowerShell execution shortly after a scheduled task was created on a workstation. The command line contains encoded content. The analyst must determine whether this is expected administration, a policy violation, or evidence of compromise.

Initial alert is not a verdict. Encoded PowerShell, an unfamiliar task, or an unusual parent process can justify investigation, but none independently proves malicious activity.

docs.title: Investigation objectives
docs.text:
1. Establish what happened and when.
  2. Identify the account, process, task definition, and affected host.
  3. Correlate independent endpoint, identity, and network telemetry.
  4. Test benign and malicious explanations.
  5. State the conclusion, confidence, evidence gaps, and recommended next steps.

docs.title: Synthetic evidence set
docs.text:
Time (UTC) Source Synthetic observation 09:12:04 Endpoint alert Encoded PowerShell execution detected on WS-TRAIN-07 09:11:58 Process telemetry powershell.exe started; parent process and full command line available 09:10:31 Task audit A scheduled task registration was recorded; task XML and registering account require retrieval 09:12:10 DNS telemetry A query was recorded shortly after process start; destination context is not yet established 09:12:18 Network telemetry One outbound connection was observed; process attribution must be corroborated

These rows are intentionally incomplete. They provide investigation leads, not proof that the task, DNS query, and connection belong to one causal chain.

docs.title: Step 1 — Preserve and scope
docs.text:
• Record the alert ID, host identifier, event source, original timestamps, collection time, and analyst actions.
  • Preserve the original event records and task definition before making changes.
  • Confirm the host owner, business function, maintenance window, and whether an approved change exists.
  • Establish whether similar activity appears on other endpoints.
  • Record which telemetry sources are available and their retention windows.

Do not modify or delete the task before preserving the relevant evidence unless an authorised containment decision requires immediate action.

docs.title: Step 2 — Reconstruct process execution
docs.text:
Review the process event and collect, where available:

  • Image path, hash, signer, and file metadata
  • Full command line and parent command line
  • Parent and child process identifiers or process GUIDs
  • User, logon session, integrity level, and host
  • Process start and termination times

Validate the parent-child relationship using the raw event. Parent process names can vary by Windows version and execution path; do not assume one fixed Task Scheduler process chain.

For Sysmon, Event ID 1 is Process Create. Its presence depends on Sysmon installation and configuration. Correlate process identifiers and timestamps rather than relying only on process names.

docs.title: Step 3 — Inspect the scheduled task
docs.text:
Retrieve the task's:

  • Full task path and name
  • Registration and modification times
  • Author and security principal
  • Trigger and execution conditions
  • Action, executable path, arguments, and working directory
  • Run level and task history
  • Creation or modification source, where available

Compare the task definition with the organisation's approved software deployment, administration scripts, and change records. A task can be legitimate, misconfigured, or unauthorised; classify it only after checking ownership and intent.

docs.title: Step 4 — Correlate independent telemetry
docs.text:
Evidence source Questions to answer Important limitation Windows process telemetry Which process launched PowerShell? What command and account were used? Collection and command-line visibility depend on configuration Task Scheduler logs / audit When was the task registered, changed, and executed? Relevant logging may not have been enabled or retained PowerShell operational logs Is script-block or module content available? Logging policy and version affect visibility DNS Which name was queried, by which host, and at what time? A query alone does not prove a successful connection Network / proxy / firewall Was a connection established? What process or host initiated it? Network records may not identify the originating process Identity logs Was the account's sign-in or privilege use expected? Correlation requires correct time and identity context File telemetry Were scripts or payloads created, modified, or executed? Absence of a file event is not proof that no file existed

Build the timeline using UTC and preserve the original timestamps. Distinguish event time from collection or ingestion time.

docs.title: H1: Approved administration
docs.text:
Supporting evidence could include a known task owner, approved change, expected script path and signature, documented execution window, and matching activity on similarly managed endpoints.

Evidence against it could include an unknown registering account, unapproved arguments, an unexpected script location, or activity outside the change window.

docs.title: H2: Unauthorised but non-malicious activity
docs.text: A legitimate user may have created a task outside the change process. This can still be a policy or control issue even when there is no evidence of malware.

docs.title: H3: Malicious persistence or execution
docs.text:
Supporting evidence could include an unexplained task, concealed or user-writable execution path, obfuscated arguments, untrusted script content, suspicious account use, corroborated command-and-control activity, or related actions on other hosts.

No single indicator is sufficient. Corroborate the task, process, identity, and network evidence.

docs.title: Step 6 — Document the conclusion
docs.text:
Use a conclusion format that separates facts from interpretation:

  • Observed: what the source records directly show.
  • Correlated: which independent records align by host, identity, process identifier, and time.
  • Interpretation: what the combined evidence suggests.
  • Alternative explanations: plausible benign or non-malicious causes considered.
  • Confidence: low, moderate, or high, with a reason.
  • Gaps: missing logs, incomplete retention, uncertain attribution, or unverified ownership.
  • Next steps: further collection, owner confirmation, remediation, or escalation under approved procedures.

Example conclusion for this training case:

The available records establish that PowerShell executed shortly after a scheduled task was registered. They do not yet establish who authorised the task or whether the outbound connection was caused by that process. The case remains unresolved pending task-definition review, account validation, and process-to-network correlation.

docs.title: Step 7 — Response considerations
docs.text:
If evidence supports compromise, follow the organisation's incident-response process. Preserve volatile and relevant endpoint evidence, identify scope, and obtain the required approval for containment actions. Do not isolate a host, disable an account, or remove a task solely because an encoded command or one suspicious event was observed.

If the activity is approved, document the owner and change reference. If it is unauthorised but not malicious, route it through the appropriate control-remediation process.

docs.title: Analyst checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Original alert and raw records preserved
  • [ ] Host, user, and time zone confirmed
  • [ ] Process and parent process reviewed
  • [ ] Scheduled task definition and owner verified
  • [ ] PowerShell logging availability checked
  • [ ] DNS and network records correlated
  • [ ] Alternative explanations considered
  • [ ] Scope and affected assets assessed
  • [ ] Confidence and evidence gaps documented
  • [ ] Response actions aligned with approved procedure

docs.title: Labs
docs.text:
Practical environments and experiments that connect cybersecurity concepts to observable system behaviour.

This section is documentation-led. A lab is described as tested only after the setup, versions, steps, and expected results have been verified. Proposed designs are reference architectures, not proof of running infrastructure.

docs.title: Featured walkthrough
docs.text: • Windows Endpoint Telemetry: Sysmon to Elastic — a safe reference design for generating, collecting, and validating a benign Sysmon process event. Reference design; not yet lab-tested.

docs.title: Infrastructure and platform
docs.text: Linux and Windows systems, virtual machines, virtual networking, storage, identity, and container fundamentals.

docs.title: Security monitoring
docs.text: A defensive stack can combine endpoint telemetry (such as Sysmon and Linux audit logs), network visibility (such as Zeek or Suricata), and central analysis (such as Elastic or Wazuh). Each integration should document resource requirements and data flow.

docs.title: Offensive security
docs.text: Isolated targets for reconnaissance, web application testing, vulnerability validation, and remediation verification. Testing remains within systems owned by the lab or explicitly authorised for assessment.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text: Repeatable tests for log generation, detection logic, parsing, network behaviour, platform troubleshooting, and security-control validation.

docs.title: Lab write-up standard
docs.text:
1. Objective, scope, and safety boundary
  2. Hardware, operating system, and software versions
  3. Architecture and network configuration
  4. Prerequisites and implementation steps
  5. Validation commands and expected results
  6. Observed output, issues, and troubleshooting
  7. Cleanup, rollback, and lessons learned
  8. References and last-reviewed date

A diagram or proposed tool list is not proof that an environment has been deployed. Each future write-up will state its status explicitly.

docs.title: Windows Endpoint Telemetry: Sysmon to Elastic
docs.text:
Reference design — not yet lab-tested

This walkthrough describes a safe, reproducible design for collecting Windows process-creation telemetry and reviewing it in Elastic. It is a build plan, not evidence that this environment has been deployed or tested. Record the exact Windows, Sysmon, Elastic Agent, Elasticsearch, and Kibana versions before marking it tested.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Generate one benign process event on an isolated Windows virtual machine, confirm that Sysmon records it, collect the event with Elastic, and verify that the event can be searched and interpreted.

Success criteria

  1. A controlled process launch produces a Sysmon Process Create event (Event ID 1).
  2. The event is visible in the local Sysmon Operational log.
  3. The configured collection agent forwards the event to the expected Elastic data stream.
  4. The event contains enough context to identify the process and its parent.
  5. The write-up records any missing fields, collection delay, and configuration limitations.

docs.title: Scope and safety
docs.text:
• Use a Windows VM that you own or are explicitly authorised to administer.
  • Use Notepad as the benign test process. Do not use malware, exploit code, credential dumping, persistence payloads, or live suspicious indicators.
  • Prefer a host-only or otherwise restricted virtual network. Permit only the management and telemetry connectivity required by your lab.
  • Do not connect this exercise to production endpoints or production SIEM data.
  • Do not paste real user, customer, or employer telemetry into public tools.

docs.title: Reference architecture
docs.text:
Windows test VM
  └─ Sysmon service
       └─ Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational
            └─ Elastic Agent (Windows integration)
                 └─ Elasticsearch
                      └─ Kibana Discover

The Elastic Windows integration documents collection of Windows-specific channels including Sysmon and PowerShell. The Sysmon data stream is named windows.sysmon_operational in the integration documentation. Confirm the actual data stream and field mappings in your own version before using saved queries.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A supported Windows 10 or Windows 11 VM with administrative access. On Windows 11, check whether the built-in Sysmon optional feature is available in your edition/build.
  • Sysmon downloaded from Microsoft's official Sysinternals page.
  • An Elastic environment with a compatible Elastic Agent and Windows integration, or an equivalent approved log collector.
  • Sufficient disk space for the VM and a snapshot taken before configuration.
  • A written record of versions, VM network mode, host name, and collection configuration.

Official references:

  • Microsoft: Enable and configure Sysmon in Windows
  • Microsoft Sysmon download and usage
  • Microsoft Sysmon event reference
  • Elastic Windows integration

docs.title: 1. Prepare the endpoint
docs.text:
1. Create or select an isolated Windows VM.
  2. Apply the updates required for the lab and record the OS build.
  3. Take a VM snapshot.
  4. Confirm the VM can reach only the required management and telemetry endpoints.
  5. Record the local time zone. Sysmon event timestamps are recorded in UTC.

docs.title: 2. Install and verify Sysmon
docs.text:
Windows 11 now offers Sysmon as a built-in optional feature, while the standalone Sysinternals download remains available. Choose one installation method appropriate to the VM and Windows version; do not install the built-in feature and standalone package on top of one another.

  1. Check whether Sysmon is already installed before making changes:
Get-Service sysmon*
  1. For Windows 11, review Microsoft's current instructions for enabling the built-in optional feature. For Windows 10, or where you deliberately choose the standalone package, download Sysmon from the official Microsoft Sysinternals page. Verify the download source and publisher.
  2. Review the current Microsoft usage instructions before installation; command-line options can change between Sysmon releases.
  3. Install or enable Sysmon with an approved configuration. For this first exercise, ensure Process Create telemetry is enabled.
  4. Open Event Viewer and navigate to Applications and Services Logs → Microsoft → Windows → Sysmon → Operational.
  5. Confirm the channel is present, Sysmon is running, and new events are being written.

Sysmon Event ID 1 records process creation, including process and parent-process context. Network connection events (Event ID 3) are disabled by default, so do not expect them unless you deliberately enable them in the configuration.

docs.title: 3. Generate a benign event
docs.text:
Open PowerShell in the test VM and run:

Start-Process -FilePath "$env:WINDIR\System32\notepad.exe" -PassThru |
    Select-Object Id, ProcessName

Close Notepad normally after confirming it started.

In Event Viewer, inspect the newest Sysmon Process Create event. Confirm that the image, process ID, command line, parent process, user, and timestamp fields are populated where available. The exact values depend on the VM and Sysmon configuration.

You can also inspect recent events with PowerShell:

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
    LogName = 'Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational'
    Id      = 1
} -MaxEvents 10 |
    Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, ProviderName, Message

docs.title: 4. Configure collection
docs.text:
In Elastic Fleet, enrol an Elastic Agent on the Windows VM and add the Windows integration according to the official integration guide. Enable the Sysmon Operational channel/data stream.

Do not assume that adding the integration proves collection is working. Check agent health, integration policy, permissions, data stream creation, and the arrival of a new event generated after the policy was applied.

If you use a different SIEM or collector, document the equivalent source channel, collection method, destination, parsing stage, and field mapping.

docs.title: 5. Search and verify
docs.text:
In Kibana Discover, select the relevant Sysmon data view and search for the test process. A starting KQL example is:

event.dataset : "windows.sysmon_operational"
and event.code : "1"
and process.name : "notepad.exe"

The integration's field mappings and dataset names can vary by version and configuration. If the query returns no results, inspect the raw event and the data view before changing the query. Do not interpret a failed query as proof that no event was generated.

For the matching event, record:

  • @timestamp and the source event time
  • event.dataset and event.code
  • host.name
  • process.name, process.executable, and process.command_line
  • process.pid and process.entity_id, if present
  • process.parent.name, process.parent.executable, and parent process ID, if present
  • user.name, if present
  • The time at which the event became searchable

docs.title: 6. Validate the collection path
docs.text:
Check Expected evidence If it fails Sysmon installed Sysmon service and Operational channel exist Review installation and service status Event generated Event ID 1 for the Notepad process Check Sysmon configuration and event time Agent healthy Agent is enrolled and policy is applied Review agent status, permissions, and connectivity Data received New Sysmon document appears in the expected data stream Check integration channel, agent logs, and ingest errors Fields usable Process and host fields are searchable Inspect the raw event and parsing/mapping Timeline consistent Source time precedes or matches ingestion time Check time zones, clock synchronisation, and pipeline delay

A local event with no corresponding SIEM document indicates a collection or ingestion problem, not a detection failure. A document with missing fields indicates a parsing, mapping, or source-configuration issue that should be diagnosed separately.

docs.title: Troubleshooting checklist
docs.text:
• Verify the Sysmon service is running and the Operational channel is enabled.
  • Confirm Event ID 1 is not excluded by the Sysmon configuration.
  • Generate a new event after the collector policy is active; do not rely only on older events.
  • Confirm the Elastic Agent policy includes the Windows integration and Sysmon channel.
  • Check agent health, network reachability, permissions, ingest pipeline errors, and data-stream naming.
  • Compare the raw event with the parsed document before changing field names in a query.
  • Check endpoint and SIEM clock synchronisation and compare source event time with ingestion time.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
1. Close the test process.
  2. If Sysmon was installed only for this exercise, remove it using the uninstall procedure documented by Microsoft.
  3. Remove or unenrol the test agent only if it is no longer required.
  4. Retain or delete lab data according to your lab retention policy.
  5. Revert the VM snapshot if you want to return to the original state.

docs.title: Evidence record
docs.text:
Before changing the status to Lab-tested, attach or record:

  • Windows edition/build and VM platform
  • Sysmon version and configuration hash or version
  • Elastic Agent, integration, Elasticsearch, and Kibana versions
  • Sanitised screenshot or export of the local Event ID 1
  • Sanitised SIEM document showing the same process event
  • Query used and exact fields observed
  • Collection delay and any troubleshooting performed
  • Cleanup result and date last verified

Current status: Reference design only. No execution results are claimed by this page.

docs.title: Learn
docs.text:
A structured learning map for the technical foundations and security workflows covered by Privacy Skill Vault.

The curriculum is organised into five connected domains. Each domain will grow through concise explanations, tested examples, exercises, and references. A topic is not described as lab-tested until it has actually been validated.

D01Infrastructure & Platform FoundationNetworking, operating systems, virtualisation, cloud, and platform fundamentals. D02Security Monitoring & DetectionTelemetry, SIEM, alert triage, detection engineering, and threat hunting. D03Offensive Security & TestingAuthorised reconnaissance, web testing, vulnerability validation, and reporting. D04Security Operations & InvestigationsInvestigation methods, evidence correlation, incident response, and cyber fraud. D05Operations, Maintenance & CapstoneReliability, automation, operational change, validation, and integrated projects.

docs.title: How to use the learning paths
docs.text:
1. Start with the domain overview and prerequisites.
  2. Work through concepts before attempting the practical exercise.
  3. Record commands, versions, expected output, and observed results.
  4. Link the exercise to a lab or investigation where relevant.
  5. Revisit the references and note limitations or environment-specific behaviour.

Content status: These pages define the curriculum and study direction. Individual topics will be expanded as complete, reviewed material is ready; the site will not use placeholder cards to imply that unfinished guides are already published.

docs.title: D01 — Infrastructure & Platform Foundation
docs.text: Understand the systems and network services on which applications and security controls depend.

docs.title: Learning areas
docs.text:
• Networking: Ethernet, IPv4/IPv6, subnetting, routing, switching, VLANs, TCP/UDP, DNS, DHCP, HTTP/S, and TLS.
  • Linux: users and permissions, processes, services, storage, filesystems, logs, SSH, and systemd.
  • Windows: accounts, services, Event Viewer, PowerShell, process creation, and basic domain concepts.
  • Virtualisation and containers: hypervisors, virtual networks, images, containers, and resource allocation.
  • Platform operations: storage, CPU and memory, backups, patching, and availability.

docs.title: Practical exercise
docs.text: Build a small isolated network with one Linux system and one Windows system. Document the addressing plan, DNS resolution, connectivity tests, user permissions, service status, and relevant system logs.

docs.title: Evidence to record
docs.text:
Environment and software versions; network diagram and private lab IP plan; commands and expected results; troubleshooting and root cause; security implications and references.

D02 uses this foundation to understand telemetry. D04 uses it to correlate endpoint, identity, and network evidence.

docs.title: D02 — Security Monitoring & Detection
docs.text: Learn how security telemetry is collected, normalised, searched, correlated, and converted into actionable detections.

docs.title: Learning areas
docs.text:
• Log sources: Windows Security, Sysmon, Linux audit logs, firewall, DNS, proxy, web, and identity events.
  • SIEM foundations: ingestion, parsing, field mapping, timestamps, retention, searches, and dashboards.
  • Alert triage: context gathering, severity, scope, false positives, escalation, and documentation.
  • Detection engineering: Sigma concepts, rule logic, exclusions, testing, and change control.
  • Threat hunting: hypotheses, data requirements, pivots, baselines, and recording findings.

docs.title: Practical exercise
docs.text:
Generate benign process and authentication activity in a controlled endpoint. Confirm that expected events are collected, identify the fields needed for a detection, test a query against available data, and document false-positive conditions.

A rule is not production-ready merely because it parses or returns results. Record the data source, tested event samples, expected matches, false positives, performance considerations, and review date.

docs.title: Applied walkthrough
docs.text: Continue with the Windows Endpoint Telemetry: Sysmon to Elastic lab. It is a reference design until the environment, versions, event output, and SIEM collection are actually verified.

docs.title: D03 — Offensive Security & Testing
docs.text: Understand common attack paths so weaknesses can be identified, validated, explained, and remediated in authorised environments.

docs.title: Learning areas
docs.text:
• Scope, rules of engagement, asset discovery, and safe test planning
  • Reconnaissance and service enumeration
  • Web application fundamentals and common vulnerability classes
  • Authentication, session management, access control, and input handling
  • Vulnerability validation, evidence capture, impact assessment, and remediation
  • Retesting and clear technical reporting

docs.title: Practical exercise
docs.text:
Use an intentionally vulnerable local application. Define the scope, identify one low-risk finding, reproduce it without accessing real user data, capture minimal evidence, explain impact, recommend a fix, and retest.

Only test systems you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Avoid destructive payloads, production data, persistence, or unnecessary service disruption.

docs.title: D04 — Security Operations & Investigations
docs.text: Develop a repeatable approach to investigating suspicious activity using evidence from endpoint, network, identity, application, and fraud-monitoring systems.

docs.title: Learning areas
docs.text:
• Alert validation, triage, prioritisation, and escalation
  • Timeline construction and event correlation
  • Endpoint process, persistence, and authentication analysis
  • Network and DNS investigation
  • Threat intelligence: relevance, confidence, age, and context
  • Cyber-fraud patterns, account takeover signals, and transaction context
  • Incident handling, evidence integrity, containment considerations, and lessons learned

docs.title: Practical exercise
docs.text:
Use a synthetic alert dataset. Define the question, preserve original evidence, normalise timestamps, correlate related events, identify what is known and unknown, and write a conclusion with confidence and next steps.

Separate observed facts from assumptions. Record data-source limitations, time-zone handling, missing telemetry, alternative explanations, and confidence.

docs.title: D05 — Operations, Maintenance & Capstone
docs.text: Connect technical security work to stable, supportable operations.

docs.title: Learning areas
docs.text:
• Service health, capacity, storage, performance, and availability
  • Patch, configuration, and vulnerability management
  • Backup, recovery, disaster recovery, and change control
  • Automation with reviewable scripts and safe failure handling
  • Operational documentation, runbooks, escalation, and handover
  • Detection and platform maintenance, tuning, and regression testing

docs.title: Capstone approach
docs.text: Choose a small, authorised lab environment and define a measurable security objective. Build the environment, generate test activity, collect telemetry, implement a detection, investigate the result, tune false positives, document operational requirements, and demonstrate recovery or rollback.

docs.title: Completion evidence
docs.text: Scope, architecture, assumptions, reproducible setup and version details, test cases and observed results, security and operational risks, recovery procedure, and lessons learned.

docs.title: Privacy and external services
docs.text:
Most parsing, extraction, and transformation features process input locally in your browser. The Threat Intel Hub is different: it sends the single indicator you submit to public third-party services only after you select Enrich Indicator. IPv4 lookups use Shodan InternetDB and RDAP; domain lookups use RDAP and Cloudflare DNS. Optional links to VirusTotal, AbuseIPDB, URLScan, and Shodan also send the indicator to the selected provider when opened.

The Threat Intel Hub does not make requests while you type. Provider responses may be incomplete, unavailable, or out of date; they are not a verdict that an indicator is malicious or benign.

Do not paste customer information, authentication data, internal logs, confidential indicators, or employer-sensitive material into this public page. Public providers may process or retain submitted indicators under their own terms and policies. Review those policies before use.

docs.title: Operational limitations
docs.text:
• Tool output is an aid to analysis, not a verdict or automated security decision.
  • The IOC extractor performs pattern-based extraction. IPv4 syntax is checked, but private/reserved classification and DNS validation are not performed; domain-like strings are not proof of registration or resolution.
  • The Event Encyclopedia contains 16 curated records, not a complete Windows or Sysmon event catalogue. Query examples and field names must be checked against your event version and SIEM schema.
  • The timestamp converter preserves sub-millisecond input remainders for Unix microsecond/nanosecond and FILETIME formats, but JavaScript Date calendar display is limited to milliseconds.
  • The YARA builder performs only a textual reference check; it is not a grammar parser or compiler. Validate rules with the YARA compiler or an approved engine.
  • The email header analyser parses supplied text. It does not cryptographically verify DKIM, SPF, or DMARC, nor establish the provenance of Authentication-Results or Received headers.
  • The severity calculator is a keyword heuristic with illustrative bands, not an approved incident severity policy, SLA, or containment decision.
  • The Sigma page currently displays source YAML only. It does not parse or validate YAML, evaluate Sigma conditions, or generate Elastic, Splunk, or Sentinel queries. Use maintained Sigma tooling for conversion, then validate the result against your SIEM schema and telemetry.
  • CVSS scoring accepts CVSS v3.1 vectors, validates required Base metrics and supported metric values, and calculates Base, Temporal, and Environmental scores using the v3.1 equations. Confirm the vector and scoring assumptions before using the result in vulnerability prioritization.
  • Detection templates are examples and must be tested and reviewed before operational deployment.
  • Results can vary with browser support, input format, data quality, and external service availability.

Use only on data you are authorised to process.
